one_liner: Vector-backed sorted set/map beating std::set on insert+remove at small sizes, up to ~256 elements.
what_it_does: flat_set/flat_map are Boost.Container's vector-backed drop-in replacements for std::set/std::map, keeping elements in one contiguous sorted array instead of a red-black tree. Lookup and positioning use binary search (O(log n) comparisons), but insertion and erasure shift elements, making those O(n). The public API mirrors std::set/std::map's associative-container interface, iterators, and comparators, so most code ports with an include and namespace change.
how_it_is_fast: Core technique is cache-friendly linear storage: a sorted vector-like sequence (default plain vector, or a user-supplied vector-like container) gives contiguous memory and random-access iterators, avoiding the pointer-chasing and per-node allocation of a red-black tree. For small containers this locality and lack of per-element allocation outweighs the O(n) shifting cost of insert/erase; std::set's balanced-tree structure only pays off once n is large enough that O(log n) tree operations beat O(n) vector shifts (crossover around 128-256 elements per the cited benchmark).
when_to_use: Sets/maps that stay small (roughly <=128-256 elements per container), even if there are many such containers
Read-mostly or lookup-heavy workloads where iteration/cache locality matters more than mutation cost
Cheap-to-move key types (ints, small PODs) where shifting on insert/erase is cheap
Existing std::set/std::map code that can tolerate iterator/reference invalidation on mutation
Memory-constrained code avoiding the per-node allocation overhead of tree containers
when_not_to_use: Large sets/maps (thousands+ elements) mutated frequently -- std::set was ~13.4x faster than flat_set at 8192 elements in the cited benchmark
Code relying on iterator/reference/pointer stability across insert/erase -- flat containers invalidate on shift/reallocation
Bulk one-at-a-time insertion of very large unsorted datasets -- GitHub issue #154 reports near-hang (100% CPU) inserting ~9M elements individually into flat_map
Workloads needing guaranteed O(log n) worst-case insert/erase (latency-bounded mutation)
Large or expensive-to-move key/value types, since every insert/erase move-shifts surrounding elements

integration.dependencies: Boost.Config, Boost.Move, Boost.Intrusive (ships as part of Boost; no separately compiled library)
integration.min_toolchain: C++03 baseline (README states C++03 support); has conditional code paths for C++11 features like initializer_list and variadic templates when available
integration.platforms: any (portable C++, no architecture-specific code observed)
integration.thread_safety: not documented -- no built-in synchronization; same external-synchronization requirement as std::set/std::map
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: same associative-container API/semantics as std::set/std::map, but different iterator/reference invalidation rules and iterator category (random-access vs. bidirectional), so algorithmic code ports directly while code depending on node stability does not

gotchas: Insert/erase invalidate iterators and references to elements after the mutation point (vector shift/reallocation), unlike std::set's per-node stability
Underlying sequence container is swappable (e.g. stable_vector, static_vector, small_vector) -- use stable_vector for reference stability at the cost of contiguity
One-at-a-time insertion of large unsorted data can effectively hang (see issue #154); prefer bulk/sorted-range construction to amortize shifting
Provides random-access iterators, so generic code that dispatches on iterator category behaves differently than with std::set's bidirectional iterators
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick flat_set/flat_map over fast-containers, S+ tree, or tlx::btree when the working set stays small (roughly <=128-256 elements) and you want a true drop-in std::set/map replacement shipped with Boost and no extra dependency; the sibling B-tree/B+tree structures target much larger n (up to 10M-scale) and win precisely in the size range where flat_set has already crossed over to being slower than std::set.
verified_claims_summary: A single-author 2014 blog benchmark (500,000 random insert-then-erase operations on int keys, -O3, compiler and hardware unstated) timed boost::container::flat_set against std::set across sizes 2-8192: flat_set was ~2.5x faster at size 2, ~1.1x faster at 128, then lost ground from 256 elements up, with std::set ~13.4x faster at 8192.
status_note: Actively maintained as a core part of Boost (repo shows a commit dated 2026-09-23) and BSL-1.0 licensed, so it is freely copyable/redistributable with no licensing friction.
